newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - June 16.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New York Times business - June 16.

text.p: * The Clinton administration appears ready to craft a new policy concerning "smut" on the Internet that would leave most on-line regulations up to the industry.

* The Netherlands, the site of an European economic gathering, has experienced prosperity, developing an economy that is between the harsh American style and the inefficiency of a traditional European welfare state.
* Airbus Industrie plans to launch two new versions of its A340 four-engine, wide-body airliner.
* Orange County, Calif., on the rebound from its bankruptcy, is again making the rounds of investment fund managers, bond-rating agencies and insurers, and seeking to get its credit rating restored.
* The tax bill recently approved by the House Ways and Means Committee is littered with so-called "invisible boomerangs," provisions that hold hidden dangers.
* DDB Needham, a unit of Omnicom Group Inc, has agreed to purchase a majority stake in DM9, a privately held Brazilian advertising agency.
* International Business Machines Corp is planning to introduce a new line of data storage products, known as Seascape.
* Nine New York area Inernet companies made a pitch at a forum for financing -- and validation.
* Voice consultants are finding plenty of business among broadcast journalists looking to hone their speaking and delivery skills.

* The first generation of hand-held computer, with the look and feel of Microsoft's Windows program, are now on the market. But analysts say they post little threat to U.S. Robotics Corp's Palm Pilot model.

* Radio Data Systems, a system that adds the printed word to radio, was introduced with fanfare to the U.S. market five years ago. But now it appears destined to follow the same slide as the eight-track tape and Beta videocassette.

* Faroudja Laboratories thought his business was doomed with the advent of high-definition TV, a system his company has sought to replicate for the past decade. But the company is now finding some broadcasters interested in using its equipment to fake HDTV.
* Personal computer makers are expected to unveil new machines called NetPCs that are meant to lower the cost of corporate computer networks.

* Compaq Computer Corp Chief Executive Eckhard Pfeiffer, hoping to avoid the pratfalls that befell his predecessor, is looking to remake the company to avoid a growing threat from rival personal computer makers.
